questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical per-tenant traffic routing, feature flag management, and end-to-end validation with minimal manifests in CNF/Kubernetes environments.

## Key Concepts
- Sidecar-based traffic routing with per-tenant control
- Namespace-scoped ConfigMap for cnf.canary.enabled and cnf.canary.sample-rate
- Deterministic hashing for consistent bucket allocation
- Minimal YAML manifests for quick validation

## Code Example

**Namespace-scoped ConfigMap:**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.canary
  namespace: tenant-a
data:
  cnf.canary.enabled: "true"
  cnf.canary.sample-rate: "5"
```

**Canary Deployment:**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: canary-resource
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: resource
    version: canary
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: stable-resource
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: resource
    version: stable
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

**Sidecar Configuration:**
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cnf-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: cnf-gateway:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: cnf-config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: cnf-config
          configMap:
            name: cnf.canary
```

## Validation
Apply the manifests and verify routing:
```bash
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
kubectl apply -f services.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

# Test canary routing
export TENANT_ID="tenant-a"
for i in {1..100}; do
  curl -H "X-TENANT-ID: $TENANT_ID" http://cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc/v2/resource
done
```

Expected: ~5% of requests route to canary-resource, 95% to stable-resource based on deterministic tenant ID hashing.

## Why This Is Asked
This question validates the ability to design per-tenant request mutation with runtime configuration, isolation, and safe rollback—a realistic pattern in CNF gateways deploying WASM filters.

## Key Concepts
- WASM sandboxing and module loading in a CNF sidecar
- Tenant-scoped policy storage with fast reloads via ConfigMap
- Validation, rollback, and observability in a live gateway
- End-to-end testing using a one-namespace manifest

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.filter.rules
  namespace: cnf-gateway
data:
  rules.json: |
    {
      "tenant1:abc123": {
        "pathRewrite": {
          "pattern": "^/v1/(.*)$",
          "replacement": "/tenant1/v1/$1"
        },
        "headers": {
          "add": {
            "X-Forwarded-Tenant": "tenant1",
            "X-Tenant-ID": "tenant1"
          }
        }
      }
    }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: cnf-gateway
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: cnf-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cnf-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: cnf-gateway
      containers:
      - name: proxy
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: wasm-filter
          mountPath: /etc/wasm-filters
        - name: rules
          mountPath: /etc/config
        env:
        - name: CONFIG_MAP_NAME
          value: cnf.filter.rules
      volumes:
      - name: wasm-filter
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: rules
        configMap:
          name: cnf.filter.rules
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests the ability to implement tenant-scoped security policies inside a CNF gateway, using Kubernetes ConfigMaps for policy storage and a sidecar for real-time evaluation. It also checks understanding of config reloads and per-request performance.

## Key Concepts

- Tenant-aware policy evaluation and path/method matching
- Sidecar design and ConfigMap-driven policy
- In-memory policy cache and reload semantics
- Path normalization and wildcard handling

## Code Example

```javascript
// Pseudo: evaluatePolicy(tenant, method, path) -> boolean
function evaluatePolicy(tenant, method, path) {
  const rules = policy[tenant] || []
  for (const r of rules) {
    if (r.method === method && (r.path === path || matches(r.path, path))) return true
  }
  return false
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you handle overlapping rules or wildcard policies across tenants?
- How would you audit and rotate policies without downtime?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests policy-as-code proficiency, practical use of Gatekeeper/OPA, and ability to derive concrete manifests and validation steps for a CNF multi-tenant setup.

## Key Concepts

- OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- ReadOnlyRootFilesystem, hostNetwork, and Privileged security controls
- Namespace-scoped policy targeting CNFs
- Lightweight test manifests to validate allow/deny paths

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (yaml)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: cnfnamespacesecurity
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: CNFNamespaceSecurityConstraint
        listKind: CNFNamespaceSecurityConstraintList
        plural: cnfnamespacesecurityconstraints
        singular: cnfnamespacesecurityconstraint
  targets:
  - target: admissionreviews
    rego: |
      package cnfnamespacesecurity
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
        some i
        input.review.object.spec.containers[i].securityContext.hostNetwork
        msg := "hostNetwork is forbidden for CNFs"
      }
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
        not input.review.object.spec.containers
        # fallback for non-pods
      }
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        some i
        input.review.object.spec.containers[i].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem != true
        msg := "readOnlyRootFilesystem is required for all containers"
      }
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.object.spec.containers[i].securityContext.privileged == true
        msg := "privileged containers are disallowed"
      }
```

```yaml
# Constraint (yaml)
apiVersion: cnfnamespacesecurity.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: CNFNamespaceSecurityConstraint
metadata:
  name: cnf-a-security
spec:
  namespace: cnf-a
```

```yaml
# Compliant Pod (yaml)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-cnf
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:latest
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      privileged: false
      runAsNonRoot: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

```yaml
# Non-compliant Pod (yaml)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-cnf
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:latest
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
      privileged: true
```

## Follow-up Steps

- Apply ConstraintTemplate, Constraint, and test manifests in a single namespace and observe denial events for non-compliant pods.
- Extend with a quick kubectl patch to simulate remediation and re-validate.
